In 1883, during Manuel Gonzalez's mandate, Mexico was submerged in another economic crisis. The coins were scarce and Gonzalez introduced nickel coins instead of the circulating silver and copper coins. The nickel coin flooded the market; however, it was rejected by the people because the stores charged double the price in order to receive nickel coins. The bakeries had two prices for the bread: a lower price for silver coins, and a higher one for nickel coins. This affected greatly the poor people, because the salaries were paid in nickel coins. The contempt was so much that even the thieves rejected the loot if it was in nickel coins.

At the end of the year, people were rioting in the streets against the nickel coin. The president was in his car during one of the riots. The rioters stopped the car and got the president off the car. The one-armed president saluted the people as he used to, raising his good arm, and had no other option but to be walked by the protesters to the palace. Some days later, the nickel coin was retired. The metal was sold off cheap in the London market.

Roeder, Ralph. Hacia el Mexico moderno: Porfirio Diaz. Mexico, FCE, 1995, page 211.
